newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New customs rules cloud ex-Moscow air cargo market.
newsitem.headline: New customs rules cloud ex-Moscow air cargo market.

text.p: Air cargo rates from Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport edged upwards in the last four weeks, but new customs rules could lessen demand for air shipments, a Reuters survey showed.
Rates per kilo to Frankfurt, London and Luxembourg from Russia's leading air cargo gateway rose to $1.15 from $1.13, to $1.21 from $1.20 and to $1.36 from $1.35 for a 100 kg shipment respectively.

Nikolai Belyaev, sales manager of EMS Garant Post, a forwarder for Air France, KLM and ANA Cargo, said a change of customs rules at Sheremetyevo could prompt shippers to seeks alternative routes -- including by sea and road instead of by air.
"Forwarders are waiting for the introduction of new rules and... the increase of customs service rates," he said.
Otherwise the market had been quiet and stable for the last four weeks.
"Rates pratically did not change in this period," Belyaev stated.

Sergei Mochalov, senior cargo manager at TCT Cargo, Aeroflot's cargo agent, said his clients had had many problems with customs at Sheremetyevo, which is legendary for its mysterious rules and delays.

Mochalov added that Aeroflot had more orders in January but would not plan to increase its cargo rates next month. But Sergei Rozdin, chief cargo manager at Aerotur, a forwarder for Aeroflot, said cargo rates inside Russia may rise soon because Russian airport tariffs had already increased.
Igor Mordvinov, senior sales manager of Burlington Air Express Moscow, said rates would rise in March.
"We have already received information about it," he said. "March will be more interesting for forwarders."
Maria Shakova, Sheremetyevo Cargo sales manager, said that her company enjoyed booming business in January.
"Cargo turnover is increasing especially in export shipments," she said, adding that her company had doubled its shipments last month compared with January 1996.
The cargo manager at British Airways said that business was steady despite a January increase in BA rates.

Meanwhile, Western air courier firms operating in Russia -- these include Federal Express, DHL, TNT and United Parcel Service -- said growing competition had resulted in lower rates in Russia where the local mail system has a poor reputation for reliability.

Fedex led the way by cutting prices from Russia to all destinations worldwide last week. The cost of sending a half-kilo letter (one pound) from Moscow to North or South America was lowered to $38 from $65.
It will now also cost $38 to send a letter of the same weight to many destinations in Western Europe, down from $60. The rate reduction also applied to heavier packages.
Ben Scott, FedEx's chief representative in Russia, said the company aimed at providing the "best service with a new price".
"We plan to add ten cities for service within the next three months in Russia," he said, adding that the company will concentrate its activity from its the Moscow market.
Last year FedEx began daily cargo service from Moscow's Vnukovo airport to Paris via Frankfurt operating a Boeing 727-200 jet.
"Recently we had several cancellations of flights (from Vnukovo airport), but only due to weather conditions. The operation of the Boeing 727 is very efficient," Scott said.
Ivan Shatskikh, UPS financial director, said that FedEx was forced to lower prices because they were too high previously.
DHL's Moscow office also said it also recently lowered rates in Russia and the former Soviet Union, where the company plans to open several new offices.

But TNT plans to move prices in the opposite direction from March 1, an official at TNT's Moscow office said but did not give details of the rate hike. TNT plans to open 23 offices in Russia, up from two at present in Moscow and St. Petersburg.
UPS also plans expansion with new offices in Minsk and Tashkent, Shatskikh said. The company already serves about 60 destinations in CIS states.
"We make shipment operating three daily charters from Moscow, St. Petersburg and Kiev using Antonov and L-410 cargo aircraft," Shatskikh said.
Rates to three key U.S. destinations -- Miami, New York and San Francisco -- were fixed at $3.38, $2.65 and $3.25 per 100 kilos respectively.
Peter Vins, president of Vinlund Air, said his company sent several large shipments to the United States, South Africa and to India during the last four weeks.
Burlington's Mordvinov said that it may be soon possible to increase shipments from Russia to South American destinations.
"Clients have been asked us about rates to Buenos Aires, Peru and Rio de Janeiro. They plan shipments in March and April," he said.
Burlington expected many shipments to India in the coming months."It will be optics, space equipment and metals," Mordvinov said.
Natasha Tebeneva, International Transport Service Japan cargo manager, said shipments between Russia and Japan were stable during January.
"Seventy five percent of our clients are Japanese firms and most of them were very active," she said. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax:5017
